pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 6–8 years

- **Topic:** Habitat Vocabulary

- **Standards — UK (DfE KS1 Year 2 'Living things and their habitats'):** supports 'identify that most living things live in habitats to which they are suited... identify and name a variety of plants and animals in their habitats, including microhabitats' — this LANGUAGE topic supplies the words (habitat, environment, microhabitat, conditions, shelter, woodland, ocean, desert, rainforest, pond) needed to describe those habitats.

- **Standards — US (no direct NGSS PE; supports 2-LS4-1 / K-ESS3-1):** the vocabulary underpins 2-LS4-1 '[curriculum wording omitted; reference 2-LS4-1]' and K-ESS3-1 (needs–habitat relationship). NGSS has no standalone vocabulary PE — note honestly.

- **Operational details:** Children learn to NAME and USE the words for where living things live and what they need there, at two scales — habitat (woodland, pond, desert) and microhabitat (under a log, in a rock pool). They apply 'adapted to', 'conditions', and 'shelter' to justify why a given animal suits a given place. Vocabulary is taught in context (matching, describing real scenes), not as isolated definitions.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier A (concrete, vocabulary-in-use). Success = correctly using 'habitat' vs 'microhabitat' with an example of each, naming three contrasting habitats and what makes each distinctive, and explaining a match with 'conditions'/'shelter'/'adapted to' rather than just labelling.
bestPractices: Teach the words in context (matching and describing real scenes) rather than as isolated definitions to memorise.
Explicitly separate the two scales — habitat (the whole place) and microhabitat (a small habitat within it) — with a worked example of each.
Distinguish 'habitat' from 'home/shelter': the habitat is the whole place; the nest/burrow is only where it shelters.
Pair each habitat word with its defining 'conditions' (wet/dry, hot/cold, light/dark) so vocabulary carries meaning, not just labels.
Use local first-hand exploration (under logs, in ponds) so microhabitat vocabulary attaches to real experience.
keyRepresentations: A labelled habitat scene (woodland, pond, hedgerow, seashore) with tappable regions.
Habitat vs microhabitat scale pair (the woodland → the log within it).
Animal–habitat matching cards annotated with 'conditions' and 'adapted to'.
A conditions word-bank (wet, dry, hot, cold, dark, damp, sunny) applied to each place.
commonMisconceptions: Using 'habitat' to mean the animal's nest or home rather than the whole surrounding place.
Not grasping the microhabitat scale — treating 'under a log' as unrelated to the woodland it sits in.
Believing any animal can live in any habitat (ignoring conditions/suitability).
Confusing 'environment' and 'habitat' as identical, or using neither with precision.
Thinking only exotic places (jungle, desert) are habitats, not a local pond or hedge.

learn.summary: Help 6–8 year olds name and USE habitat vocabulary (habitat, environment, microhabitat, conditions, shelter, woodland, ocean, desert, rainforest, pond) in context rather than reciting definitions. Two scales matter: the whole habitat (woodland, pond, desert) and the microhabitat nested inside it (under a log, a rock-pool crevice). Children justify why an animal suits a place using 'conditions', 'shelter' and 'adapted to'. Teach through describing real scenes and matching, and anchor 'microhabitat' to first-hand local exploration where possible.

activities.title: Explore a labelled habitat scene and 'lift the log'
feedback: If a child calls the nest the 'habitat', point from the single nest out to the whole wood: the habitat is the whole place that holds many creatures; the nest is only its shelter.
If a child treats 'under the log' as unrelated to the woodland, trace the nesting physically — point from the log out to the whole wood — and say the microhabitat sits inside the habitat.
If a child names the place but not its conditions, prompt with 'The conditions here are ___ and ___' to attach words like wet, dry, dark, damp, sunny.
activities.rationale: Interactive labelled scenes with reveal-and-zoom make the habitat→microhabitat scale visible and let vocabulary attach to a pictured place rather than an abstract definition. The zoom from log to woodlice is an optional interaction example that makes the nesting concrete; a confusable-pair flap (habitat vs shelter) can target the common home/habitat slip. These are illustrative mechanisms, not required technology; a printed cross-section picture with a fold-out flap can serve the same purpose.
sourceClaims: DfE KS1 Year 2 'Living things and their habitats' statutory includes identifying and naming plants and animals in their habitats including microhabitats, and that living things live in habitats to which they are suited.
learnerActions: Look at a cross-section countryside-to-coast picture holding woodland, pond, hedgerow and seashore.
Point to or tap each place, say its name, and state its conditions (a pond is wet; a wood is often shady and damp; a seashore is salty and windy; a hedgerow is sheltered and leafy).
Name one animal that lives in each place and say what it needs there (food, water, shelter, space).
'Lift the log' or zoom into a small damp, dark spot of woodlice and centipedes, and name it a microhabitat — a small habitat sitting inside the bigger woodland.
Compare the whole place (habitat) with one specific nest or burrow (shelter), saying aloud which word fits which.
activities.intendedInsight: A habitat is the whole place that supports many living things; a microhabitat is a smaller habitat nested within it; a shelter/nest is only the one spot where an animal hides. Each place has defining conditions that make it suit particular animals.

activities.title: Match animals to habitats and justify with conditions
feedback: For a wrong match, give a conditions hint: 'a cactus needs dry, sunny conditions — would a wet pond suit it?'
If a child sorts by size of animal rather than scale of place, re-focus on the place: is this the whole surrounding area, or a small spot within a larger one?
activities.rationale: Active matching with a required justification makes vocabulary productive and surfaces the suitability idea, countering the belief that any animal can live anywhere. Dragging cards and immediate conditions hints are optional interaction examples; paper cards work equally well.
learnerActions: Match living-thing cards (animals and plants) to habitat scenes (cactus, a plant→desert; crab→rock pool; fox→woodland; frog→pond).
For each match, add a 'why?' using 'conditions', 'adapted to' or 'shelter' (e.g. 'a cactus is adapted to dry, sunny conditions').
Test a deliberately wrong pairing (cactus→pond) and explain why the conditions do not suit it.
Sort a second set of cards into 'whole habitat' vs 'microhabitat inside it'.
activities.intendedInsight: Not every living thing can live in any place; a match is justified by the conditions a place offers and what the plant or animal is adapted to. The habitat/microhabitat sort reinforces the two scales.

activities.title: Describe a habitat aloud using the target words
feedback: If 'habitat' and 'microhabitat' are used interchangeably, make the nesting physical: point from the crack (microhabitat) out to the whole pool (habitat).

If 'conditions' means only 'the weather', scaffold with a frame — 'The conditions in a rock pool are ___ and ___' — to attach it to wet, salty, cold. Treat this as a word that needs exercise, not a misconception.
For the bird's nest question, accept that a nest is most precisely the bird's shelter, not the whole habitat; use it to re-separate shelter from the surrounding place.
Encourage transfer: ask the child to describe a second, contrasting habitat using the same words.
activities.rationale: A spoken-description task elicits spontaneous, contextual use and distinguishes a child who owns the words from one who can only recite. This is a teaching activity as well as a check; keep the focus on how words are used, not on definitions.
sourceClaims: DfE KS1 Year 2 'Living things and their habitats' statutory includes identifying and naming plants and animals in their habitats including microhabitats, and that living things live in habitats to which they are suited.
learnerActions: Look at a rock pool or woodland picture.
Describe the place aloud: where a crab (or other animal) lives, what it is like there, and where it can hide.
Use whichever words fit while narrating: habitat, microhabitat, conditions, shelter, environment.

Answer follow-up prompts: point to a microhabitat inside the habitat; name the conditions that make a rock pool hard to live in; use 'environment' in a sentence about the seashore; decide whether a bird's nest is a habitat, a microhabitat or just a shelter, and why.
activities.intendedInsight: Meaning is shown by correct USE in running description — naming the whole place as the habitat/environment, a crevice as a microhabitat within it, the specific conditions (wet, salty, cold, pounding waves), and the animal's shelter — not by reciting definitions.

activities.title: Meet an animal who describes its home
feedback: If the child names only the shelter, ask for the whole surrounding place too.
Prompt for at least one named condition before moving on.
activities.rationale: A talking-animal prompt offers a playful, responsive way to rehearse the words; it suits oral practice and motivation. It is an alternative with a different purpose — open prompting — complementing the anchored-visual work rather than replacing it.
learnerActions: Listen to or read an animal persona describing where it lives and asking 'where do I live, and why does it suit me?'
Name the animal's habitat and the conditions it needs.
Point out a microhabitat within the habitat where the animal might find shelter, and say how the microhabitat and the shelter differ from the whole habitat.
activities.intendedInsight: The same vocabulary can be rehearsed through dialogue, prompting a child to supply habitat, conditions and shelter for a described animal.

constraints: Teach the words in context (matching and describing real scenes), not as isolated definitions to memorise.
Explicitly separate the two scales — habitat (the whole place) and microhabitat (a small habitat within it) — with a worked example of each.
Distinguish 'habitat' from 'home/shelter': the habitat is the whole place; the nest or burrow is only where an animal shelters.
Pair each habitat word with its defining conditions (wet/dry, hot/cold, light/dark) so vocabulary carries meaning.
Use local first-hand exploration (under logs, in ponds) where possible so microhabitat vocabulary attaches to real experience; include local ponds and hedges, not only exotic places.

Recognition and matching tasks support vocabulary but do not by themselves elicit independent spoken or written use; include at least one task where the child produces running description with the target words.
Reveal/zoom/drag mechanisms and flaps are illustrative examples of interaction; printed pictures, fold-outs and paper cards can achieve the same goals.

Success criteria: correctly use 'habitat' vs 'microhabitat' with an example of each, name three contrasting habitats and what makes each distinctive, and explain a match using 'conditions'/'shelter'/'adapted to' rather than just labelling.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The source marks the NGSS 2-LS4-1 citation as unverified and notes NGSS has no standalone vocabulary performance expectation; this vocabulary supports but is not itself an NGSS PE. The NGSS claim was removed from activity sourceClaims because it supports the topic, not a specific teaching principle. Treat standards alignment as supportive context, not tested claim.

The retained DfE claim grounds the statutory curriculum content (naming in habitats including microhabitats, suitability); it justifies WHAT is taught but does not establish that any proposed interaction, medium or scaffold is effective or superior to another.

The legacy source asserted that open dialogue and a 3D world teach vocabulary less well than a labelled scene. These are catalog-ranking preferences, not established comparative efficacy; they have been softened to scoped affordance statements (dialogue suits oral rehearsal; navigation may add overhead without serving naming) and the dialogue activity is retained as a purposeful alternative.

The original 'is a bird's nest a habitat or a microhabitat?' probe implies a binary; a nest is most precisely a shelter, so graders should accept 'neither — a shelter'. This has been made explicit in the prompt and feedback.

probeDeeper: You used 'habitat' — can you point to a microhabitat inside it? Give me one.
What conditions make a rockpool a hard place to live?
Use 'environment' in a sentence about the seashore.
Is a bird's nest a habitat or a microhabitat? Why?
assess.correctAnswer: Uses the terms accurately in running description: the rockpool/seashore is the habitat or environment; a crevice under a rock is a microhabitat within it; names the conditions (wet, salty, cold, pounding waves); identifies the crab's shelter (under a rock, in a crack). Meaning is shown by correct USE in context, not by reciting definitions.

errorPatterns.pattern: Uses 'habitat' to mean the single home or den — 'the crab's habitat is its shell/hole'.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Contrast the whole rockpool (habitat) with the one crack the crab hides in (its shelter/microhabitat); the habitat holds many creatures, not one.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Applies 'habitat' to the exact spot one animal sits in rather than to the whole place that supports many organisms.

errorPatterns.pattern: Uses 'habitat' and 'microhabitat' interchangeably — no sense that one is nested inside the other.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Make the nesting physical: point from the crack (microhabitat) out to the whole pool (habitat); microhabitat = a small habitat within a bigger one.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Calls the whole seashore a microhabitat, or a single crack a habitat, with no scale distinction.

errorPatterns.pattern: Avoids or empties 'conditions' — either doesn't use it, or uses it to mean only 'the weather'.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Scaffold with a frame — 'The conditions in a rockpool are ___ and ___' — to attach the word to wet/salty/cold; the concept is present, the word needs exercise. Do not treat as a misconception.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Describes the scene vividly but never characterises it with 'conditions', or says only 'the weather is nice'.

responseLevels.gap: Uses the words as loose synonyms (habitat = home), avoids 'microhabitat' and 'conditions', or applies them wrongly.
responseLevels.full: Uses all the terms accurately and spontaneously in context, distinguishing habitat from microhabitat by scale and applying 'conditions' to specific physical features, then transfers the vocabulary to a second, contrasting habitat.
responseLevels.partial: Uses 'habitat' and 'shelter' correctly but blurs the habitat/microhabitat scale, or uses 'conditions' only vaguely.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Show a picture of a rockpool at the seaside (or a woodland). Say: 'Describe this place to me — where a crab lives, what it is like there, and where it can hide. As you talk, use whichever of these words fit: habitat, microhabitat, conditions, shelter, environment.' Listen for how the words are used, not for definitions.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who only half-owns the words uses 'habitat' as a bare synonym for 'home', cannot separate habitat from microhabitat by scale, and skips or misuses 'conditions'. Correct use reveals the nested scale (a microhabitat sits inside the habitat) and applies 'conditions' to physical features — something a definition-reciter usually cannot do while narrating.
